extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and instructors learning plain English style and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Concise, prescriptive style rules and principles for producing plain, vigorous English prose (usage, punctuation, sentence and paragraph composition, and common word-usage pitfalls). Intended to guide drafting and revision of written English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's. Follow this rule whatever the final consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Charles's friend", "Burns's poems", "the witch's malice". Exceptions: possessives of ancient proper names in -es and -is, the possessive "Jesus'", and idioms like "for conscience' sake". Many constructions may be recast as "the X of Y" (e.g., "the heel of Achilles"). Note that pronominal possessives (hers, its, theirs, yours, oneself) have no apostrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a comma in a series (Oxford comma)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "red, white, and blue"; "gold, silver, or copper"; "He opened the letter, read it, and made a note of its contents." Usage note: the Government Printing Office and Oxford University Press follow this. In names of business firms the final comma is omitted (e.g., "Brown, Shipley & Co.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas (or between comma and period at sentence end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interruption to the flow is slight the commas may be omitted, but never insert one comma and omit the other. If a parenthetic expression is preceded by a conjunction, place the first comma before the conjunction. Always-parenthetic items include: (1) year/day when part of a date, (2) abbreviations like etc. and jr., (3) non-restrictive relative clauses and similar clauses indicating time/place. Distinguish non-restrictive (set off with commas) from restrictive clauses (no commas). Related constructions: setting off phrases or dependent clauses that precede/follow the main clause. Avoid setting off independent clauses by commas (see Rule 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma before a conjunction that introduces a coordinate (independent) clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "The early records of the city have disappeared, and the story of its first years can no longer be reconstructed." Similar two-part sentences with connectives like as (because), for, nor, while (in sense 'and at the same time') require a comma. If the second member is introduced by an adverb (not a conjunction), use a semicolon (see Rule 5). The connectives so and yet may function as adverbs or conjunctions; avoid colloquial uses of so. If a dependent clause or introductory phrase precedes the second independent clause, no comma is needed after the conjunction. When the subject is the same for both clauses and is expressed only once, use a comma if the connective is but; if the connective is and, omit the comma when the relation is close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not join independent clauses by a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not join grammatically complete independent clauses with just a comma; use a semicolon (or period) instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: use semicolon or period: "Stevenson's romances are entertaining; they are full of exciting adventures." If a conjunction is used, use a comma (see Rule 4). If the second clause is preceded by an adverb (accordingly, besides, then, therefore, thus) and not by a conjunction, use a semicolon. Exceptions: very short parallel clauses may take a comma ("Man proposes, God disposes"); colloquial forms sometimes use a comma (appropriate only in dialogue, familiar letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not break sentences in two
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using periods where a comma (or other close punctuation) is required — do not fragment sentences unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of faults: "I met them on a Cunard liner several years ago. Coming home from Liverpool to New York." (should be comma). It is permissible to use a short sentence for emphasis when warranted ("No reply."), but be certain emphasis is intentional and not a punctuation or syntax error. Rules 3–6 cover key principles of ordinary sentence punctuation and should be mastered.

rubrics_metrics.name: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence begins with a participial phrase, that phrase must grammatically modify the sentence's subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faulty: "Walking slowly down the road, he saw a woman..." (walking refers to he, not the woman). Recast to make the modifier refer to the correct subject: "He saw a woman... walking slowly down the road." Applies also to participial phrases preceded by conjunctions or prepositions, nouns in apposition, and adjective phrases. Sentences violating this rule are often ludicrous; recast for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paragraph the unit of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the paragraph as the unit of composition — ordinarily one paragraph per topic; subdivide a subject into topical paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very brief subjects a single paragraph may suffice. Aim to aid the reader: the paragraph's beginning signals a new step in development. Extent of subdivision varies with composition length; examples given for book notices, poem reports, novels, historical events. Avoid single-sentence paragraphs except for transitions or dialogue (each change of speaker begins a new paragraph). After writing a paragraph, examine whether subdivision will improve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin each paragraph with a topic sentence; end it in conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, begin paragraphs with a topic sentence and make the following sentences develop that statement; end to reinforce or follow the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally useful paragraph structure: (a) topic sentence at/near start; (b) succeeding sentences explain, establish, or develop it; (c) final sentence emphasizes the topic or states a consequence. Avoid ending with digressions or unimportant details. Transitional sentences relating the paragraph to what precedes may precede the topic sentence (set apart as separate paragraph if more than one). Methods of developing the topic sentence: restatement, definition, denial of contrary, illustration, proof, implication. Examples (narrative, exposition) illustrate variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the active voice because it is more direct and vigorous than the passive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example improvement: "I shall always remember my first visit to Boston" better than passive "My first visit to Boston will always be remembered by me." Passive is not forbidden — use when convenient or necessary. Avoid chaining passives (one passive depending on another). Avoid making the subject of a passive a noun that expresses the entire action leaving the verb perfunctory (recast: "This region was surveyed in 1900" rather than "A survey of this region was made in 1900"). Habitual use of the active makes writing forcible; substitute active verbs for weak constructions (replace "there is/there were" forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Put statements in positive form
rubrics_metrics.description: Express assertions positively; avoid colorless, hesitant, or evasive negatives. Use "not" for denial or antithesis, not evasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer positive phrasing: instead of "He was not very often on time" write "He usually came late." Replace negatives with positive equivalents (not honest → dishonest; did not remember → forgot). Use negative words other than not sparingly; they can be strong ("The sun never sets upon the British flag"). Antithesis is effective: "Not charity, but simple justice."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definite, specific, concrete language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer specific, definite, concrete terms to general, vague, abstract ones to arouse and hold reader attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "It rained every day for a week" instead of "A period of unfavorable weather set in." Specific details enable the reader to project into the scene. Even in exposition/argument, supply particular instances. Cites literary examples (Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Browning) showing power of concreteness. Quoted theoretical support notes that thought is particular and specific terms create immediate images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous writing is concise: avoid unnecessary words, phrases, and clauses; make every word tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists common unnecessary expressions and suggested revisions: "the question as to whether" → "whether"; "there is no doubt but that" → "no doubt"; "used for fuel purposes" → "used for fuel"; "he is a man who" → "he"; avoid "the fact that" (revise out). Use active voice and positive statements to be concise. Combine serial simple sentences into one complex sentence when appropriate. Numerous before/after examples show large word savings by compression and recombination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing long stretches comprised mainly of loose (paratactic) sentences of similar form; this becomes monotonous and tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loose sentences of the type two co-ordinate clauses with conjunctions (and, but, so, who, which, when, where, while used non-restrictively) in sequence produce sing-song rhythm and emptiness. Recast some into simple sentences, semicolon-joined sentences, periodic sentences, or varied clause structures to remove monotony. Compare weak paragraph example to stronger prose to see effects. Vary sentence structure to maintain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form (parallel construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of similar function/content should have outwardly similar grammatical form so readers readily perceive the likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of faulty vs corrected parallelism: "Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method, while now the laboratory method is employed." → better: "Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method." Ensure articles/prepositions that apply to a series are either used only before the first term or repeated before each term ("the French, the Italians, the Spanish, and the Portuguese"). Correlative expressions (both…and, not only…but also, either…or, first, second) should be followed by the same grammatical construction. Multiple illustrative corrections provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related words together
rubrics_metrics.description: Place words that belong together (logically modify the same element) close together to avoid ambiguity and misattachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misplaced modifiers cause confusion or ludicrous meanings; recast sentences so modifiers are adjacent to the words they qualify. Applies to participial phrases, adjectives, adverbials, and other modifiers. Examples in the book illustrate recasting to correct misplacement (see rules on participial phrases and related clauses).

rubrics_metrics.name: In summaries, keep to one tense
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing a work or series of events, maintain a single consistent tense throughout the summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching tenses in summaries confuses readers and undermines cohesion. Use an appropriate tense (often present for plot summaries) and apply it consistently to the recitation of events or the account of a work's content. Keep temporal perspective fixed unless there is a deliberate rhetorical reason to shift tense; examples in the book demonstrate proper usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange sentence elements so that emphatic words or phrases appear toward the end of the sentence, where emphasis naturally falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The end of the sentence is the position of emphasis; place the most important words there. Recast sentences to move the focal element to the close for stronger effect. Examples and comparisons in the text show how placement changes emphasis and force.
